22.title: The boy at the door
22.hook: Parvati shapes a son from earth and breathes life into him; why families welcome Ganesha into clay
22.carry: the holy can live in clay
22.tomorrow: the boy says no to the next one at the door. who is it?
22.howItsDone: At Ganesh Chaturthi many families bring home a clay Ganesha, invite him in with prana pratishtha, and after a day and a half to ten days immerse the image in water (visarjan). His birth story is often retold then.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the first camp on a battlefield, with Krishna's line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Now the stories start, and the first one starts at a closed door.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Parvati lives with Shiva on Mount Kailash, and every guard at the door is one of his ganas, his attendants, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants in, they step aside. Nobody in that house is simply hers. So before her bath she takes the paste she rubbed on her skin, the earth of her own body, and shapes a boy. Then she breathes life into him. The first face he ever sees is his mother's. She hands him a staff and gives him one job: guard this door. No one comes in.
screen: `NOBODY IN THE HOUSE IS HERS.` → `A BOY SHAPED FROM EARTH.` → `SHE BREATHES LIFE INTO HIM.` → `NO ONE COMES IN.`

segments.voice: That boy grows up to be Ganesha, the god you met on day one. This telling is the Shiva Purana's, a collection of stories about Shiva, and it isn't the only version. Notice what he's made of. Not thunder, not light. Earth, shaped by the Goddess's hands, with her breath in it. Hindu homes still act this story out. Every year at Ganesh Chaturthi, many families bring home a Ganesha shaped from clay. With prayers they invite him to live in it, a rite called prana pratishtha: setting the breath in. For a few days he's the guest of honor, fed, sung to, visited by the whole street. Then they carry him to a river or the sea, and give the clay back to the water. The teaching under it: God can be welcomed into something as ordinary as earth, and loved there, without being trapped there. That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: God isn't only far off in the sky. God can be found in what's right in front of you, even a handful of earth. And somewhere down the mountain, someone very large is walking home.
screen: `EARTH, SHAPED BY THE GODDESS.` · `GANESH CHATURTHI: A GOD OF CLAY.` · `PRANA PRATISHTHA: SETTING THE BREATH IN.` · `BACK TO THE WATER.` · then, large: `THE HOLY CAN LIVE IN CLAY.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, pick up something ordinary near you that matters to you: a ring, a mug, a photo. Hold it. Notice that it's just stuff, and also not. Something you love has been breathed into it. Then set it down gently. It's still yours.
Ganas: Shiva's attendants, the guards of his house. Keep an eye on them. The boy made of earth is going to end up leading them.
screen: `GANAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the holy can live in clay. Parvati shaped hers from earth. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 22 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO WALKS UP TO THAT DOOR?`

23.title: Shiva comes home
23.hook: the fight; the head; Parvati's grief stops the universe
23.tomorrow: Shiva has to bring the boy back. so where does he find a head?
23.howItsDone: Hindus tell this story as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi, carrying both the weight of Parvati's grief and the mending that follows.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ganas: Shiva's guards, and a boy made of earth with one job. Some things need a guard. Someone is about to test that.
screen: `SOME THINGS NEED A GUARD.`

segments.voice: Here's a comment you might see under a video of a Ganesha festival: wait, his own dad cut his head off? Fair question, and the story has an answer. Why would a story like that be told at a festival full of kids? Start where it starts. Shiva walks home up the mountain to his own house, and at his own door is a boy he has never seen. You can't come in, says the boy. This is my house, says Shiva. My mother said no one. Shiva sends his ganas. The boy beats them back. In the Shiva Purana, even the gods can't get past him. Then Shiva raises his trident.
screen: `WAIT, HIS OWN DAD?` → `A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.` → `THE TRIDENT.`

segments.voice: So, the puzzle. The story doesn't hide what happens, and it doesn't make anyone the villain. The boy is keeping his word to his mother. Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Both are right, and something terrible happens anyway. Family fights can look like that. Then Parvati comes out. In the Shiva Purana her grief is so big that she calls up fierce goddesses, forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe. Heaven starts coming apart. The sage Narada and the gods come pleading, the same gods who couldn't get past the boy at the door, and she names her terms: bring my son back, and give him honor among you. Otherwise, no universe. That's the answer. This isn't a story about a god losing his temper. It's about what comes after. Grief is taken seriously; nobody tells this mother to calm down. And the one who broke it has to mend it. Shiva, often honored as the one who destroys so things can begin again, now has to help something begin again. Mended doesn't mean unbroken. The boy won't come back the same. But he comes back.
screen: `BOTH OF THEM ARE RIGHT.` · `HER GRIEF STOPS THE UNIVERSE.` · `THE ONE WHO BROKE IT MENDS IT.` · then, large: `WHAT BROKE CAN BE MENDED.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Write down one thing in your life that broke, a friendship, a promise, a habit, in a few plain words. Under it, write one small step that could start a mend: not a fix, just a start. Then fold the paper; keep it or toss it, because writing it was the point, and nobody else has to see it.
Trident: Shiva's three-pointed spear, trishula in Sanskrit, three spears. A weapon raised at a door, and the start of a long mending.
screen: `TRIDENT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this one: what broke can be mended, not unbroken but mended. Day twenty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 23 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DOES HE FIND A HEAD?`

24.title: The elephant facing north
24.hook: the search; the head; the boy lives
24.tomorrow: two brothers race around the world. how does the slow one win?
24.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin weddings, housewarmings, new ventures and other ceremonies by honoring Ganesha first, often with a short prayer or mantra to him before anything else begins.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trident, and a grief that stopped the universe until Shiva agreed: what broke can be mended. Now, the mending itself.
screen: `WHAT BROKE CAN BE MENDED.`

segments.voice: Every family has a story two relatives tell differently, each sure the other got it wrong. Ganesha's head is one of those, and here the relatives are old texts. Here's the Shiva Purana's telling. Go north, Shiva tells his ganas. Bring back the head of the first living creature you meet. They run down the mountain into the forests, and the first creature they find is an elephant. Shiva sets its head on the boy's body and breathes life into him. The boy opens his eyes for the second time in his life, and his mother is there again. Now he has a trunk, wide ears, and the face you already know.
screen: `TWO RELATIVES, TWO VERSIONS.` → `GO NORTH.` → `AN ELEPHANT.` → `HE OPENS HIS EYES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Now the debate, and it's a real one among people who love him. Why an elephant? One side says: the text's answer is plain. It was the first creature they met. The head is chance, and the point of the story is what Shiva does next. The other side says: look at that face. Big ears, to listen more than he speaks. A trunk that can uproot a tree or pick up one grain of rice. An elephant doesn't go around the forest; it walks through and makes a path. That fits a remover of obstacles too well to shrug off. And the texts don't even agree on how the head was lost: in the Brahmavaivarta Purana, it happens when Shani, the god of the planet Saturn, looks at the baby. The tradition keeps both tellings side by side. The fair move in a debate like this is to say the other side's view first, at its best, before your own. What they share is the ending. Shiva makes the boy leader of the ganas, the very guards who fought him: Ganesha, Ganapati, lord of the ganas. And he promises the boy will be worshipped first, before any god, before any ceremony. So a wedding, a housewarming, a new business often begins with Ganesha. The newest god goes first.
screen: `WHY AN ELEPHANT?` · `ONE SIDE: THE FIRST CREATURE MET.` · `THE OTHER: THAT FACE FITS.` · `WORSHIPPED FIRST, BEFORE ANY GOD.` · then, large: `FIRST, BEFORE ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Count slowly on your fingers: three things that broke and came back different, but whole. A friendship after a fight, a body after an injury, you after a hard year. For each finger, name who or what helped mend it, and give a quiet thank-you; some people say that thank-you to God.
Ganesha: lord of the ganas. The boy who fought the guards ends up leading them, with an elephant's face and first place at every beginning.
screen: `GANESHA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: first, before anyone. Shiva's promise to the boy at the door. That's day twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 24 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DOES THE SLOW ONE WIN?`

25.title: The race around the world
25.hook: Ganesha vs Kartikeya: one circles the earth, one circles his parents
25.tomorrow: so why is one of Ganesha's tusks snapped short?
25.howItsDone: Hindus walk pradakshina, a clockwise circle keeping the holy on their right, around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire; this story is often told to children to explain why parents are honored.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesha: a new face, and a promise to be honored first, before anyone. Today he gets a brother, and a race.
screen: `FIRST, BEFORE ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Your phone counts every step you take. It has no idea which ones mattered. Here's a race about that. Two brothers: Kartikeya, the warrior, fast and bright on his peacock, and Ganesha, round and patient on his mouse. Their parents, Shiva and Parvati, set a contest: whoever goes around the whole world first, wins. Kartikeya is gone before the sentence ends, over mountains, over oceans. Ganesha looks at his mouse. The mouse looks at Ganesha. Then Ganesha walks to his mother and father and, slowly, walks one circle around them. He bows. I'm done, he says.
screen: `YOUR PHONE COUNTS STEPS.` → `A PEACOCK AND A MOUSE.` → `HE CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.`

segments.voice: Kartikeya lands, out of breath, to find his brother already declared the winner. In the Shiva Purana, Ganesha explains: the scriptures say that walking around your parents with devotion is the same as walking around the earth. My world is right here. In some readings he circles them seven times, bowing each time. That walk has a name, pradakshina: circling something holy, keeping it on your right. Hindus do it around temple shrines, sacred trees, and the fire at a wedding. It's the body saying: this is the center, and I move around it. So it isn't a trick. The tellings differ on the prize. In the Shiva Purana it's who marries first. In a telling from South India it's a single fruit of wisdom, and Kartikeya, called Murugan there, leaves home for a hill: Palani, in Tamil Nadu, where pilgrims still climb to his temple. Same race, a different ending, depending on who tells it. And Kartikeya isn't the fool. He really went around the world. Ganesha just noticed that the world he cared about was a few steps away.
screen: `MY WORLD IS RIGHT HERE.` · `PRADAKSHINA: CIRCLING THE CENTER.` · `A WEDDING, OR A FRUIT.` · `KARTIKEYA ISN'T THE FOOL.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD IS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can, and pick a center: a chair, a plant, a photo of someone you love. Walk slowly around it, keeping it on your right, one step for each breath, and feel your feet do what Ganesha's did. Notice the floor under each foot, and how your shoulders turn so the center stays on your right. As you go, name the few people who are your whole world. If standing isn't possible right now, trace a slow circle with one finger around their names.
Pradakshina: the circle walked around something holy, keeping it on your right. One brother circled the earth. The other circled his parents.
screen: `PRADAKSHINA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Something to keep from the race: the whole world is close, sometimes a few steps away. Until tomorrow.

26.title: The broken tusk
26.hook: the pen breaks mid-Mahabharata; he snaps his tusk to finish
26.tomorrow: a god this big gets around on what, exactly?
26.howItsDone: Ganesha is honored as a patron of writing and learning; some Hindus write a line honoring him at the top of a new notebook or account book before they begin.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina: a slow circle around the people who are your world. The whole world is close. Now look closely at his face.
screen: `THE WHOLE WORLD IS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Somewhere in your phone's notes there's a draft you've opened a dozen times and never finished. Hold that thought, and look at a Ganesha statue. Count the tusks. One is whole. The other is snapped short, and often he's holding the broken piece in his hand. It's a writer's story. The sage Vyasa has a vast poem in his head, the Mahabharata, and needs someone to write it down as he speaks. Ganesha says yes, on one condition: once I start, you can't stop. Vyasa adds his own: you can't write a line until you understand it. They begin. Somewhere in the middle, with the poem nowhere near done, the pen breaks.
screen: `THE DRAFT YOU NEVER FINISHED.` → `COUNT THE TUSKS.` → `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND.` → `THE PEN BREAKS.`

segments.voice: He can't stop; that was his own rule. So, the story goes, he snaps off his own tusk, dips it in the ink and keeps writing. That's why he's called Ekadanta, the one with one tusk. Now a fact worth telling someone tonight: this scribe scene is told at the start of the Mahabharata in some versions of the text, but the modern critical edition, built by comparing manuscripts, leaves it out. The tusk as a pen is a later telling still, and some Puranas explain the broken tusk with a fight against the warrior-sage Parashurama. So hold it as a story, not a record. And look what it holds for an ordinary week. Two rules keep each other honest: don't stop, and understand before you write. Tradition says Vyasa slipped in knotty verses to buy himself a breath. Then the tool breaks, and the work doesn't. Ganesha gives up something of his own, something permanent, so the thing gets finished. The remover of obstacles meets a broken pen, and the answer is himself. Half-finished things pile up: a letter, a course, a drawer. The story never says it'll be easy. It says finish the thing.
screen: `EKADANTA: ONE TUSK.` · `A STORY, NOT A RECORD.` · `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND FIRST.` · `THE TOOL BREAKS. THE WORK DOESN'T.` · then, large: `FINISH THE THING.`

segments.voice: Pick one small unfinished thing you can close in two minutes: a reply you owe, a dish in the sink, the last line of a note. Do it now, while the sit runs, start to end, without making it perfect. If it can't be done from where you are, write its first step down, and let that count. Done is the whole goal here.
Ekadanta, from eka, one, and danta, tooth or tusk: the name Ganesha earned by breaking his own tusk to keep writing.
screen: `EKADANTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line to take with you: finish the thing, even if the tool breaks. Twenty-six days in.

27.title: The mouse
27.hook: a mountain of a god rides a mouse
27.tomorrow: he's always got a sweet in his hand. what is it, and why?
27.howItsDone: In Hindu temples and home shrines a god's vahana often sits facing the deity; at Ganesh Chaturthi Ganesha's mouse is placed at his feet, sometimes with its own small offering.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ekadanta: a tusk snapped so the writing wouldn't stop. Finish the thing. Now look down, at his feet.
screen: `FINISH THE THING.`

segments.voice: The credits at the end of a movie roll for minutes: drivers, caterers, the person who held the microphone on a pole. Plenty of people have left by then. Here's an old picture that stays for the credits. Ganesha: big belly, elephant head, four arms, sitting like a king. And under him, carrying all of it, a tiny mouse, often looking up, sometimes nibbling a sweet. It makes no physical sense at all. So, one question for today: who's really doing the lifting?
screen: `NOBODY STAYS FOR THE CREDITS.` → `A BIG GOD. A TINY MOUSE.` → `WHO'S DOING THE LIFTING?`

segments.voice: In this tradition, gods have animals that carry them. Shiva rides Nandi, the bull. Vishnu rides Garuda, the great eagle. Durga rides a lion. Saraswati has her swan. Kartikeya, from the race, has his peacock. The word is vahana, from the Sanskrit root vah, to carry. A vahana is the one that carries, a mount, and it says something about its god: people read the bull as strength, the eagle as speed, the lion as courage. So why give the remover of obstacles the smallest of them all? Hindus give more than one answer. One: a mouse gets in everywhere, through walls, under doors, into the grain store. It finds a way in where nothing bigger could, which is the remover of obstacles' whole job. Two: the mouse is desire, restless and nibbling. Ganesha doesn't kill it. He rides it and steers it. The wanting stays; it just stops being in charge. Stories of where the mouse came from vary across the Puranas, and none is the official one. What they share is the picture, and its answer to the question. The god honored first, before anyone, is carried by the creature most people chase out of the kitchen. The god sits on top. The mouse does the lifting. Small carries large.
screen: `VAHANA: THE ONE THAT CARRIES.` · `THE MOUNT SAYS WHO THE GOD IS.` · `GETS IN ANYWHERE, OR RIDES DESIRE.` · `THE STORIES VARY.` · then, large: `SMALL CARRIES LARGE.`

segments.voice: Pick up, or look hard at, one small object that holds up something bigger: a key, a phone charger, one screw in the chair under you. Look at it for the whole sit, as if you'd never seen it before, and turn it over once in your hand if you can. Notice how much would stop working without it, and give it the credit nobody does.
Vahana: the one that carries, the animal each god rides. From vah, to carry. Ganesha's is the smallest of them all, a mouse.
screen: `VAHANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: small carries large, under every god and most good days. Day twenty-seven, carried.

screen: `DAY 27 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT'S THE SWEET IN HIS HAND?`

28.title: Modak
28.hook: why he's always eating; the sweet as a gift that returns
28.tomorrow: who would try to eat the sun for breakfast?
28.howItsDone: At temples and home shrines Hindus offer food to the deity and then share it as prasad; at Ganesh Chaturthi many families make modaks, offer them to Ganesha, and give them out to family and neighbors.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, vahana: a mouse under a god, doing the lifting. Small carries large. Today closes Ganesha's week, with the sweet in his hand.
screen: `SMALL CARRIES LARGE.`

segments.voice: Leave a wedding or a festival and sometimes someone presses a little box into your hands: something sweet for the road. Ganesha has his own, and he never seems to put it down. In many images there's a sweet in his hand, a modak: a little dumpling of rice flour, pinched shut at the top like a flower bud, filled with coconut and jaggery. One of his names means the one who loves modaks, and at his festival, Ganesh Chaturthi, families make them by the trayful. People tell a story about that appetite. Kubera, a rich god proud of his wealth, throws Ganesha a feast to show off. Ganesha eats every dish, every pot, and he's still hungry.
screen: `A LITTLE BOX FOR THE ROAD.` → `A DUMPLING LIKE A FLOWER BUD.` → `A FEAST THAT CAN'T FILL HIM.`

segments.voice: What finally fills him is tiny: a handful of plain food, given with love. The story isn't in one fixed text; it's the kind families pass down. But it points at the word prasad: grace, a gift given freely. At a temple or a home shrine, food is offered to the god, sits before the image a while, then comes back and is shared with everyone there. Not leftovers. The same food, returned as a blessing. People often take it with the right hand, or with both hands cupped. And a detail worth repeating: in older Sanskrit, prasada also means clarity, a calm and settled mind. The gift and the grace are one word. Now hold the week up to the light. A boy of earth, guarding a door. A trident, and a grief that stopped the universe. A new face, honored first. A slow circle around the people who are your world. A broken tusk, and the thing finished. A mouse carrying a mountain. And a sweet, handed back. Seven days with one god.
screen: `A HANDFUL, GIVEN WITH LOVE.` · `PRASAD: GRACE, GIVEN FREELY.` · `OFFERED, THEN HANDED BACK.` · `A WEEK WITH GANESHA.` · then, large: `THE OFFERING COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: If there's anything to eat near you, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a square of chocolate, hold it and smell it before anything else. Break it in two, and set half aside for someone before you taste yours. Eat your half slowly, and notice what it's like to taste something you've already given away. Some people first offer a meal to God; others offer it to the person across the table.
Prasad: grace. Food offered, then handed back as a blessing, made to be shared. The last word of the week.
screen: `PRASAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Last line of Ganesha's week: the offering comes back. Seven days, seven stories, one god.
